doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Teaching simplicity: Charlie Parker and Giant Steps
summary: He tells students to perceive simplicity, thinks in sound and color, and says Giant Steps is just three scales.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You preceded one of my questions which I think is terrific, and the thought process and how much jazz pedagogy can be in your head now, and how much it actually helps. So a big part of your life has been teaching. Is part of what you think your task is is to make things as simple for your students as possible?

Well actually if you — it’s a perception. If you can perceive the simplicity, that’s where it’s at. If you take Charlie Parker, who I haven’t heard anybody in jazz surpass that. If you break down each little fragment of his stuff it’s something simple, but the way he puts that all together is profound. You know. And I tell my students, “Can you play a B major scale?” [Nods head] “Can you play a G major scale?” [Nods yes] “Can you play E flat major scale?” Um hum. I say then you can play “Giant Steps” because “Giant Steps” isn’t nothing but three scales. You’ve got to learn to sequence them but that’s all it is. You’ve got to sequence those colors. I think more in terms of sound and color than I do notes, and of course I always put rhythm first. Rhythm is the most important thing and that’s what’s lacking in most students.
